text: The Science: Your nerves need potassium to fire and reset (NIH, 2022), yet most of us eat less than the recommended amount: only about 3 in 10 Americans reach it (Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee, 2024). In a diet trial, people who took in more potassium and less salt had better mood and less fatigue (Torres, et al, 2008), and potassium supplements eased mood and behavior problems in 13 of 16 children taking steroid drugs, which mimic the stress hormone cortisol (Pariury, et al, 2019). People who eat more of it also tend to think and remember better as they get older (Na, et al, 2022), though not every study agrees, and none yet shows extra potassium helping people who already get enough. Some people need more than others, too, since diarrhea, diuretics and some inherited kidney conditions drain it (NIH, 2022; Cruz, et al, 2001). More potassium also brings high blood pressure down (Aburto, et al, 2013), which matters on Strategy A, since its salts bring their own sodium. Stone Age diets are estimated to have had more than four times the potassium we eat now (Sebastian, et al, 2006), so eating closer to a paleo diet probably does more than adding a couple of potatoes, but the potatoes and greens below are the easy way to start. If you have kidney disease or take a blood pressure drug that holds on to potassium, like an ACE inhibitor or an ARB, ask your doctor first, since potassium can build up in your blood (NIH, 2022).
reader: someone with trauma or in withdrawal who is anxious, wired, numb or foggy, following the protocol's diet and electrolyte steps and wanting to know why each one is there

checked.point: low potassium (common in high stress) makes the KCNQ brakes fail, and eating potassium puts them back
checked.found: the brain keeps the potassium around its neurons within tight limits whatever the blood does (Hladky and Barrand 2016)
checked.still_needed: no: the brakes story is cut, with its two labels (blocks 104 and 105)

checked.point: most people eat less potassium than recommended
checked.found: 28% of Americans aged 1 and up are above the Adequate Intake (DGAC 2024, Table D.1.6)
checked.still_needed: yes: they learn they are probably low and the step is for them

checked.point: more potassium goes with better mood
checked.found: urinary potassium went with less fatigue and a lower sodium-to-potassium ratio with less anger and depression (Torres et al. 2008); potassium chloride helped 13 of 16 children with corticosteroid-induced neuropsychiatric effects (Pariury et al. 2019, retrospective)
checked.still_needed: yes: they learn what raising potassium may do for their mood

checked.point: more potassium goes with better thinking and memory
checked.found: higher intake went with higher cognitive scores and less memory decline in 4,213 Chinese adults aged 50 and up (Na et al. 2022); against: Cherbuin 2014, Zingales 2025
checked.still_needed: yes: they learn it may help their thinking, with the limit

checked.found: diarrhea, vomiting and diuretics cause hypokalemia (NIH 2022); Gitelman syndrome wastes it (Cruz et al. 2001)
checked.still_needed: yes: they check whether they are among those who need more

checked.point: eating more potassium brings high blood pressure down
checked.found: in trials, systolic pressure fell about 3.5 mm Hg, in people with high blood pressure (Aburto et al. 2013)
checked.still_needed: yes: they learn why it matters with the salts of Strategy A

checked.point: Stone Age diets had far more potassium; a paleo diet probably does more than adding potatoes (his view)
checked.found: 400 +/- 125 mEq a day in retrojected Stone Age diets (Sebastian et al. 2006)
checked.still_needed: yes: they can eat closer to a paleo diet, with the potatoes and greens as the start

checked.point: kidney disease and drugs that keep potassium in can let it build up
checked.found: ACE inhibitors and ARBs can lead to hyperkalemia (NIH 2022); restricting potassium slowed neuropathy in kidney disease (Arnold et al. 2017)
checked.still_needed: yes: they ask their doctor first if either applies to them

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")?
